assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of differentiated-product demand and dynamic industry models changed empirical industrial organisation. It is now standard in merger review, antitrust, trade and regulatory analysis. The method links theory to real market data in a way I regard as an outstanding example of useful theory tested on data.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995) is the clearest core. Pakes's wider programme (dynamic games, Ericson-Pakes, estimation methods) makes him the central figure. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important but more separable contributions, so a three-person prize on the BLP demand-estimation core with Pakes as anchor is the cleanest.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1980s-1990s and has decades of validation and wide use. There is no timing obstacle.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit Pakes alone or to include Bresnahan.
The field has no earlier laureate for empirical IO, so relative field priority is uncertain.
I rely on my own knowledge of the attribution split and have not verified sources.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models reoriented trade theory and empirics. They explain exporter selection, intra-industry reallocation and gains from trade beyond the Krugman framework. The framework is highly influential and widely taught.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the foundational model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and Helpman's broader programme complete the core. Redding has made major quantitative and spatial contributions that extend the framework, but he is later and more extension-oriented.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation and extension. The empirical foundations, including Bernard-Jensen facts, are mature.
uncertainties: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited on this ballot, though they contributed closely related work.
Overlap with other trade candidates, including quantitative models and Helpman's political-economy work, could split support.
Some trade-prize timing issues remain after the 2008 award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a pillar of modern game theory and applied theory. It underlies models of labour, trade negotiations, contracting, and decentralised markets. Its relevance to financial contracting and renegotiation is direct.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the decisive contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky (1985, 1990) on bargaining in markets is the natural second part. Binmore's contributions (Binmore-Rubinstein-Wolinsky 1986, and work on the Nash program and Ståhl-Rubinstein links) are real but secondary.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with four decades of consolidation. The delay reflects the wide field of competing theorists, not any doubt about the contribution.
uncertainties: Whether Wolinsky or Binmore is the better second laureate.
Game theory has been recognised often (Nash, Selten, Harsanyi, Aumann, Schelling, Myerson, Milgrom, Wilson), so the committee may see saturation.
Ståhl's earlier model leads to a priority question that I have not verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave a systematic framework linking electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal outcomes, backed by credible empirical testing. It is a broad, coherent research programme with large influence on political economy, public finance and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini (the 2000 book, joint papers on electoral rules and fiscal outcomes) and Besley's work on state capacity, accountability and politics in development make a coherent trio. Attribution is relatively clean across this group.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than twenty-five years of cumulative work and replication. It is partly overlapped by the 2024 institutions prize.
uncertainties: The 2024 institutions prize may make the committee reluctant to reward a neighbouring area so soon.
Possible conflicts of interest from personal and committee ties are disclosed in the protocol and not adjudicated here.
The empirical support for some cross-country results is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and the financial accelerator explain how credit frictions amplify and propagate shocks. They are central to macro-finance and crisis analysis and to policy, and rest on financial contracting ideas I know well.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is the key formal contribution on credit cycles. Bernanke-Gertler (1989) and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist (1999) are the accelerator papers. Because Bernanke is already a laureate (2022), Gertler is the natural remaining name, and Gilchrist is a secondary contributor.
assessment.maturity: Mature and very widely used in DSGE and policy models. Empirical validation is solid but not uniform.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) may limit appetite.
Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian ballot, so credit may be split.
Whether Kiyotaki-Moore is considered the more fundamental innovation relative to the accelerator.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and policy impact. The work has strong influence on public policy and on how empirical public and labour economics is done.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure across the mobility, taxation and neighbourhood work. Hendren is a close collaborator on neighbourhood effects and the marginal value of public funds. Friedman and Katz contributed significantly to specific projects, so it is difficult to find a clean boundary.
assessment.maturity: The research is recent (largely 2014 onward). Core findings have been replicated and extended, but long-run validation of the policy conclusions is not complete.
uncertainties: Maturity relative to prizes in the field.
Collaborative team structure complicates a three-name limit.
Descriptive measurement versus causal identification, and debate about neighbourhood effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based approach to technology and the China trade shock reshaped how economists understand labour demand, wage polarisation and the local costs of trade. The policy relevance is large and the findings changed the trade-adjustment debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to tasks and polarisation. The China shock papers are Autor-Dorn-Hanson. Katz's earlier skill-premium work with Autor and others is also relevant, and the task framework has other major contributors (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) not credited here.
assessment.maturity: The China shock work is from about 2013 and has survived considerable scrutiny, though debate continues about magnitude and mechanisms.
uncertainties: The task framework has contributors outside the list, which complicates attribution.
Re-examinations of the China shock estimates and long-run adjustment.
Two distinct programmes (technology and trade) may be seen as an artificial bundle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work took adverse selection from theory to quantifiable welfare analysis in actual insurance markets. It develops tests for asymmetric information, measures selection and moral hazard, and informs health-insurance policy. The link between contract theory and data is strong, which suits a corporate-finance perspective.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading empirical figures, and Salanie's methodological and conceptual contributions on testing for asymmetric information are early and important. Chiappori-Salanie (2000) is a precursor. Credit across a broad literature may be diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Substantive body of work from about 2000 to the present. Some policy findings are still being refined, so the field is less settled than the older candidates.
uncertainties: Relative weight of Finkelstein's health-economics work versus the selection papers.
Younger candidates compared with older ones with a longer track record.
Whether the committee sees the set of results as a single discovery.
